_readme.purpose: Single source of truth for every factual claim shown by the site.
rules: Render a fact as verified only when verified is true and primary_url is present.
Every displayed fact tag links to its Almanac record.
Time-sensitive facts show an as-of date and link to the live official page.
Never fill a null field with a guess.

facts.text: The Apollo 11 and Apollo 14 laser retroreflector arrays each contain 100 corner-cube reflectors of 3.8 cm; the Apollo 15 array contains 300.
facts.kid_text: Apollo 11 and 14 each left a tray with 100 tiny reflector cubes. Apollo 15's tray has 300!
facts.verification_notes: The prior source was secondary. Exact Apollo array sizes still need confirmation in a NASA primary source; excluded from story copy.

facts.text: Lunar laser ranging shows the Moon is moving away from Earth at about 3.8 cm per year.
facts.kid_text: The Moon drifts away from Earth about 3.8 cm every year.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on the NASA GSFC-supported ILRS lunar laser ranging page. The fingernail comparison from the supplied file is a site-created analogy and is omitted.

facts.text: The reflector needs no power, which is why it kept working long after other instruments left on the Moon went silent.
facts.kid_text: Retro has no battery. A reflector can bounce a laser pulse without using electrical power.
facts.verification_notes: The source in the supplied file is secondary and broadly worded. A separate, verified fact about newer passive retroreflectors is available as F-060.

facts.text: Spirit and Opportunity each had a planned mission lifetime of 90 sols (Martian days).
facts.kid_text: Both rovers were planned to work for 90 Martian days.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on NASA Spirit and Mars Exploration Rover mission material.

facts.text: Spirit became stuck in soft soil on May 1, 2009.
facts.kid_text: On May 1, 2009, Spirit got stuck in soft Martian soil.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on NASA Science Spirit mission page.

facts.text: Spirit last communicated with Earth on March 22, 2010; NASA ended recovery efforts in May 2011.
facts.kid_text: Spirit's last message arrived in March 2010. NASA ended attempts to reach it in May 2011.
facts.verification_notes: Last communication and official recovery end are kept separate in the wording.

facts.text: Opportunity was active until its last communication on June 10, 2018, more than 14 years after landing in January 2004.
facts.kid_text: Opportunity worked for more than 14 years, though it was planned for just 90 Martian days.
facts.verification_notes: Uses the requested correction: more than 14 years to last contact. NASA's official mission-end announcement was in February 2019.

facts.text: A planet-wide dust storm cut off Opportunity's solar power. NASA made its final contact attempts on Feb. 12 and announced the mission's end on Feb. 13, 2019.
facts.kid_text: A huge dust storm covered Opportunity's location. NASA's final tries to hear from it were in February 2019.
facts.verification_notes: Previously a placeholder; now verified against NASA's mission-end announcement. Final commands were sent Feb. 12; NASA announced the mission end Feb. 13.

facts.text: Ingenuity was designed for up to five experimental test flights over 30 days.
facts.kid_text: Ingenuity was designed to fly up to five test flights in 30 days.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on NASA Science Ingenuity mission page.

facts.text: Ingenuity completed 72 flights over nearly three years on Mars.
facts.kid_text: Ingenuity flew 72 times!
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on NASA Science Ingenuity mission page.

facts.text: Ingenuity made its final flight on January 18, 2024; rotor-blade damage during landing left it unable to fly.
facts.kid_text: After its final flight, rotor-blade damage meant Ingenuity could no longer fly.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on NASA Science and JPL end-of-mission release.

facts.text: InSight landed on Mars on November 26, 2018.
facts.kid_text: InSight landed on Mars on November 26, 2018, carrying a seismometer.
facts.verification_notes: Date appears on the NASA InSight mission record.

facts.text: InSight detected 1,319 marsquakes; its mission ended after dust reduced its solar power and the lander ran out of energy.
facts.kid_text: InSight recorded 1,319 marsquakes. Dust lowered its solar power until it ran out of energy.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on NASA's end-of-mission report.

facts.text: Scientists continue to analyze data gathered by InSight.
facts.kid_text: Scientists are still studying InSight's data today.
facts.verification_notes: The supplied wording is too broad for present-tense display. Omitted until tied to a specific current NASA report.

facts.text: Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977.
facts.kid_text: Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on the NASA Voyager mission page.

facts.text: NASA says Voyager 1 is expected to reach one light-day from Earth on November 18, 2026.
facts.kid_text: NASA says Voyager 1 is expected to reach one light-day from Earth on November 18, 2026.
facts.verification_notes: The previously conflicting date is now stated by NASA/JPL. Static copy only says expected; link to live NASA page for updates.

facts.text: Apollo 12 astronauts landed near Surveyor 3, visited it, and returned some of its parts to Earth.
facts.kid_text: Apollo 12 astronauts visited Surveyor 3 and brought some of its pieces home.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on the NASA Surveyor 3 mission page.
Original placeholder preserved. Specific location/condition details for the parked Lunar Roving Vehicles still need a direct NASA primary citation.

facts.text: Three Lunar Roving Vehicles were driven on the Moon: one each on Apollo 15, 16, and 17.
facts.kid_text: Three lunar rovers explored the Moon: Apollo 15, 16, and 17 each had one.
facts.verification_notes: NASA NSSDCA lists the three lunar vehicles and the Apollo missions on which they were driven.

facts.text: The lower half of the Lunar Module, called the descent stage, remained at each of the six Apollo lunar landing sites.
facts.kid_text: At each Apollo Moon landing site, the Lunar Module's lower half stayed behind.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on the NASA Apollo landing-sites page.

facts.text: Apollo 12's ALSEP was designed to remain on the Moon and send long-term scientific and engineering measurements back to Earth.
facts.kid_text: Apollo 12 left an experiment package on the Moon to send measurements back to Earth.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed in NASA's Apollo 12 press kit.

facts.text: Apollo astronauts deployed lunar laser retroreflectors, and laser-ranging measurements between Earth and the Moon continue to use surface reflectors.
facts.kid_text: Reflector arrays left by Apollo crews help researchers measure the Earth–Moon distance with laser pulses.
facts.verification_notes: ILRS/NASA page documents Apollo reflectors and ongoing lunar laser ranging; status is dated.

facts.text: NASA's lunar artifact catalog records Apollo ascent-stage impacts and other mission hardware at lunar impact sites.
facts.kid_text: Some spacecraft parts were deliberately sent into the Moon after their missions.
facts.verification_notes: Use only documented events and avoid guessing unknown impact coordinates.

facts.text: Surveyor 3 landed in 1967, sent back 6,326 television pictures, and later became the site of an Apollo 12 visit.
facts.kid_text: Surveyor 3 sent thousands of pictures before Apollo 12 astronauts came to visit it.
facts.verification_notes: NASA Science Surveyor 3 page.

facts.text: Lunar retroreflectors need no power or maintenance to reflect laser pulses.
facts.kid_text: A retroreflector can bounce a laser pulse without a battery or moving parts.
facts.verification_notes: NASA describes the passive retroreflector design; this general statement does not claim every Apollo array is currently returning useful measurements.

facts.text: Sojourner spent 83 days exploring Mars on a planned seven-day mission; the last data from Pathfinder arrived September 27, 1997.
facts.kid_text: Sojourner's planned seven-day Mars mission lasted 83 days.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on NASA's Pathfinder/Sojourner resource.

facts.text: Spirit landed in Gusev Crater on January 4, 2004, and its last communication arrived March 22, 2010.
facts.kid_text: Spirit explored Gusev Crater for more than six years before its last signal.
facts.verification_notes: NASA mission page and NASA technical report agree on landing and last communication.

facts.text: Opportunity landed in Meridiani Planum on January 25, 2004, and last communicated on June 10, 2018.
facts.kid_text: Opportunity's final message came from Meridiani Planum in June 2018.
facts.verification_notes: Landing and last communication are stated on NASA mission material.

facts.text: Curiosity launched on November 26, 2011, landed in Gale Crater on August 6, 2012, and remains an active NASA mission.
facts.kid_text: Curiosity is still exploring Gale Crater; it landed there in 2012.
facts.verification_notes: NASA Science and JPL identify Curiosity as active/current; status date is displayed.

facts.text: The Viking landers ran three biology experiments, but their results did not provide clear evidence of living microorganisms in the tested soil.
facts.kid_text: Viking tested Martian soil for signs of life, but its tests did not find clear evidence of living microbes.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed on NASA Viking mission page.

facts.text: Viking 2 landed at Utopia Planitia on September 3, 1976; its lander mission ended April 11, 1980.
facts.kid_text: Viking 2 worked at Utopia Planitia for more than three years.
facts.verification_notes: NASA Viking mission page.

facts.text: InSight landed on November 26, 2018, and its mission ended in December 2022 after dust reduced solar power and its batteries ran out of energy.
facts.kid_text: Dust covered InSight's solar panels, its power fell, and NASA ended the mission in 2022.
facts.verification_notes: NASA end-of-mission announcement and mission record.

facts.text: Ingenuity completed the first powered, controlled flight on another planet on April 19, 2021.
facts.kid_text: Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
facts.verification_notes: NASA Science mission page.

facts.text: Mars Polar Lander and the Deep Space 2 probes were lost on arrival in December 1999; an investigation found a likely landing-signal error that shut down the engines too early.
facts.kid_text: NASA lost contact with Mars Polar Lander as it arrived. Investigators found a likely signal error that may have caused a crash.
facts.verification_notes: NASA says the cause was most likely; retain that uncertainty in the wording.

facts.text: Voyager 1 is an active extended mission in interstellar space; NASA updates its distance and instrument status on the live mission page.
facts.kid_text: Voyager 1 is still sending science from interstellar space. NASA's live page tracks it.
facts.verification_notes: Status is time-sensitive; direct live page link supplied.

facts.text: Voyager 2 is an active extended mission in interstellar space; NASA updates its distance and instrument status on the live mission page.
facts.kid_text: Voyager 2 is still sending science from interstellar space. NASA's live page tracks it.
facts.verification_notes: Status is time-sensitive; direct live page link supplied.

facts.text: Pioneer 10's last signal was received on January 23, 2003; NASA says its power source had degraded below the level needed for detectable transmissions.
facts.kid_text: NASA last heard Pioneer 10 in January 2003. Its power source had faded too much for a signal to reach Earth.
facts.verification_notes: NASA Science last-signal report.

facts.text: Pioneer 11's last transmission was received in September 1995, and NASA ended the mission that month.
facts.kid_text: NASA last heard from Pioneer 11 in September 1995.
facts.verification_notes: NASA Science Pioneer last-signal report.

facts.text: Pioneer 10 and 11 were designed for missions lasting about two years, then continued operating far beyond that plan.
facts.kid_text: Pioneer was planned for about two years, but both spacecraft kept exploring for decades.
facts.verification_notes: NASA Science Pioneer mission resource.

facts.text: NASA's current Pioneer source describes Pioneer 10 and 11 as silent spacecraft; it does not provide a live distance reading, so this site does not guess one.
facts.kid_text: Pioneer 10 and 11 are no longer in contact with Earth. NASA's page does not give a live odometer reading.
facts.verification_notes: The user's brief asks for distance; no live NASA distance source was located during this build. Exact distance omitted and listed in TODO.

facts.text: Planetary protection rules help limit biological contamination of other worlds and protect Earth from material returned from space.
facts.kid_text: Planetary protection helps keep Earth germs from confusing space science, and helps keep returned samples carefully controlled.
facts.verification_notes: Paraphrase of NASA planetary protection requirements.

facts.text: NASA describes orbital debris as a collision risk to spacecraft; hardware on a planetary surface is a different issue from debris orbiting Earth.
facts.kid_text: A broken object circling Earth can hit a spacecraft at high speed. Hardware sitting on the Moon or Mars is a different kind of leftover.
facts.verification_notes: The distinction is editorial paraphrase grounded in NASA's orbital-debris definition and risk description.

facts.text: NASA says the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle's wire-mesh wheels were chosen in part because solid or air-filled rubber tires would have been much heavier.
facts.kid_text: The Moon buggy's wire wheels helped save precious payload mass.
facts.verification_notes: This is a documented example of mass shaping hardware design; do not generalize it as the reason all objects were left behind.

facts.text: Mercury's NASA fact-sheet card: diameter 4,879 km; average distance from the Sun 57.9 million km; 0 known moons in the fact sheet; day length 4,222.6 hours.
facts.kid_text: Mercury: 4,879 km wide, 57.9 million km from the Sun, 0 moons listed, and a 4,222.6-hour day. One fun fact: its listed day is longer than its 88-day year.

value.amazing_fact: Its listed day is longer than its 88-day year.

facts.verification_notes: Moon count is reported as listed in the NASA fact sheet accessed on this date; counts can change.

facts.text: Venus's NASA fact-sheet card: diameter 12,104 km; average distance from the Sun 108.2 million km; 0 known moons in the fact sheet; day length 2,802.0 hours.
facts.kid_text: Venus: 12,104 km wide, 108.2 million km from the Sun, 0 moons listed, and a 2,802-hour day. Its solar day is about 117 Earth days.

value.amazing_fact: Its solar day is about 117 Earth days.

facts.verification_notes: Moon count is reported as listed in the NASA fact sheet accessed on this date; counts can change.

facts.text: Earth's NASA fact-sheet card: diameter 12,756 km; average distance from the Sun 149.6 million km; 1 known moon in the fact sheet; day length 24.0 hours.
facts.kid_text: Earth: 12,756 km wide, 149.6 million km from the Sun, 1 moon listed, and a 24-hour day. One fun fact: it is the only planet in this set with a known moon count of one.

value.amazing_fact: NASA's fact sheet lists one moon.

facts.verification_notes: Moon count is reported as listed in the NASA fact sheet accessed on this date; counts can change.

facts.text: Mars's NASA fact-sheet card: diameter 6,792 km; average distance from the Sun 228.0 million km; 2 known moons in the fact sheet; day length 24.7 hours.
facts.kid_text: Mars: 6,792 km wide, 228 million km from the Sun, 2 moons listed, and a day just under 25 hours.
facts.verification_notes: Moon count is reported as listed in the NASA fact sheet accessed on this date; counts can change.

facts.text: Jupiter's NASA fact-sheet card: diameter 142,984 km; average distance from the Sun 778.5 million km; 115 known moons listed by NASA; day length 9.9 hours.
facts.kid_text: Jupiter: 142,984 km wide, 778.5 million km from the Sun, 115 moons listed, and a speedy 9.9-hour day.

value.amazing_fact: Its listed day is only 9.9 hours.

facts.verification_notes: The NASA Jupiter Moons page lists 115 officially recognized moons. Counts can change.

facts.text: Saturn's NASA fact-sheet card: diameter 120,536 km; average distance from the Sun 1,432.0 million km; 293 confirmed moons as of August 2026; day length 10.7 hours.
facts.kid_text: Saturn: 120,536 km wide, 1,432 million km from the Sun, 293 moons listed as of August 2026, and a 10.7-hour day.

value.amazing_fact: NASA's fact sheet lists a 10.7-hour day.

facts.verification_notes: NASA's Saturn Moons page states 293 confirmed as of August 2026. Counts can change.

facts.text: Uranus's NASA fact-sheet card: diameter 51,118 km; average distance from the Sun 2,867.0 million km; 29 known moons as of August 2026; day length 17.2 hours.
facts.kid_text: Uranus: 51,118 km wide, 2,867 million km from the Sun, 29 moons listed as of August 2026, and a 17.2-hour day.

value.amazing_fact: NASA's fact sheet lists a 17.2-hour day.

facts.verification_notes: NASA's Uranus Moons page states 29 known as of August 2026. Counts can change.

facts.text: Neptune's NASA fact-sheet card: diameter 49,528 km; average distance from the Sun 4,515.0 million km; 16 known moons; day length 16.1 hours.
facts.kid_text: Neptune: 49,528 km wide, 4,515 million km from the Sun, 16 moons listed, and a 16.1-hour day.

value.amazing_fact: NASA's fact sheet lists a 16.1-hour day.

facts.verification_notes: NASA Neptune Facts page states 16 known moons. Counts can change.

facts.text: Pluto's NASA fact-sheet card: diameter 2,376 km; average distance from the Sun 5,906.4 million km; 5 known moons in the fact sheet; day length 153.3 hours. Pluto is a dwarf planet.
facts.kid_text: Bonus dwarf planet Pluto: 2,376 km wide, 5,906.4 million km from the Sun, 5 moons listed, and a 153.3-hour day.

value.amazing_fact: Pluto is a dwarf planet, not one of the eight planets.

facts.verification_notes: Moon count is reported as listed in the NASA fact sheet accessed on this date; counts can change.

facts.text: As of November 1, 2026, NASA's live Voyager table listed Voyager 1 at about 16.07 billion miles (172.86 AU) from Earth.
facts.kid_text: As of November 1, 2026, Voyager 1 was about 16.07 billion miles from Earth. Its live NASA odometer keeps moving.
facts.verification_notes: Dynamic NASA data table; recheck at publication and preserve the as-of label.

facts.text: As of November 1, 2026, NASA's live Voyager table listed Voyager 2 at about 13.44 billion miles (144.59 AU) from Earth.
facts.kid_text: As of November 1, 2026, Voyager 2 was about 13.44 billion miles from Earth. Its live NASA odometer keeps moving.
facts.verification_notes: Dynamic NASA data table; recheck at publication and preserve the as-of label.

facts.text: Gravity on the Moon is about one-sixth of Earth's gravity.
facts.kid_text: Gravity on the Moon is about one-sixth of Earth's gravity.
facts.verification_notes: Confirmed by NASA Moon Q&A and NSSDCA Moon fact sheet.
